meta.title: Sifnos
meta.subtitle: A Self-Styled Local's Guide (From Afar)
meta.description: My favourite beaches, tavernas, bars and flavours — all in one place.

beaches.label: Beaches
beaches.intro: Sandy, pebble and rocky shores — my favourite spots for a swim on the island.
beaches.windTip: When the north wind (meltemi) picks up, head to Faros, Vathi or Platy Gialos — they face South-East or South-West and stay calm. Always ask locals about the weather too.

items.name: Kamares
items.description: The main beach at the port. Handy for a last swim before catching the ferry. On the beach you'll find Old Captain — one of the few beach bars that have kept their authentic character. Coffee and backgammon.

items.name: Glyfo / Vlycho
items.description: Walk through Faros beach to get there — it's about 3 minutes on foot.
items.tips: From here a short path leads to the Chrysopigi church, about 15 minutes on foot. Along the way you'll pass an abandoned ore-loading platform — a remnant of the mining operations that once took place on the island.

items.name: Fasolou
items.description: On the road to Faros, look for the sign to turn left before reaching the harbour and parking area. Nice beach, mostly attracts families.

items.name: Platy Gialos
items.description: The most organised beach on the island, with two beach bars: Lost Bay and Palmira. Of the three large beaches (Kamares, Vathi, Platy Gialos), this one has the most going on.

items.name: Vathi
items.description: A large beach facing south-west. The nicest spot if you have your own parasol is in front of the 'Elies' hotel, where there's plenty of space to spread out. There are also beach bars nearby if you prefer a sun lounger. Good tavernas for a meal afterwards: Okeanida and Tsikali.

items.name: Chrysopigi (Saures)
items.description: A small sandy cove beside the famous Panagia Chrysopigi church. Worth visiting for the atmosphere of the place. The beach is on the right side of the church as you face it. A dive off the rocks directly opposite is non-negotiable.

items.name: Cherronisos
items.description: A small sandy beach with a jetty for diving. Probably the most picturesque fishing village on Sifnos. If you stay until sunset, climb up to Agios Georgios (15 minutes from the square — you can drive halfway) for views towards Serifos. There's a gate — open it without hesitation and go in.

items.name: Fykiada
items.note: Accessible only by trail or boat
items.description: One of the cleanest beaches on the island, tucked in the south. The hike is fairly flat (3.2 km, about 50 minutes) and the trail is fully signposted. From June, small boats also run from Platy Gialos and Kamares.
items.tips: Start from the road to Vathi (about 2 km before you reach it). The path is clearly marked — you won't get lost.

items.name: Vroulidia
items.description: Not recommended. The rocks underwater are slippery and the road down has an extremely steep gradient. If you do go, leave the car at the top.

items.name: Kastro (Seralia)
items.description: A small beach below the village of Kastro. Not recommended.

items.name: Poulati
items.description: One of my favourite rocky spots. A short dirt road leads to a small descent (5 minutes with steps). Crystal-clear turquoise water — reminiscent of Paxos.
items.tips: Swim to the left of the rock formation in the water — that's where the pebble seabed and the most vivid turquoise colour are.

items.name: Chrysopigi (rocky side)
items.note: Rocks to the right of the church
items.description: The flat rocks to the right of the Panagia Chrysopigi church (as you walk down) make for perfect sunbathing and diving spots. A must.

items.name: Kastro (Eptamartiros church)
items.description: A similar experience to Chrysopigi but with fewer people and slightly trickier rock access.

items.name: Cherronisos (rocky coast)
items.description: A charming fishing village at the northernmost tip of Sifnos. Beautiful rocky coastline, typically quiet. Park on the square and walk to the rocks.

drinks.label: Drinks
drinks.intro: From sunset cocktails in Kastro to after-hours in Apollonia — my go-to spots for drinks on Sifnos.

items.name: Cavo Sunrise
items.description: Go for the sunset or later. Chilled-out music, generous pours and the owner Kyrios Kostas (who calls himself the Che Guevara of Sifnos) is a true character.
items.note: Not the tidiest place — but YOLO.

areas.intro: The alley (steno) of Apollonia is the heart of the nightlife. Plenty of options depending on your mood.

items.name: Botzi
items.description: Rooftop bar in the alley of Apollonia. One of the main choices for drinks with a view.

items.name: Cosi
items.description: Another rooftop in the alley, similar vibe to Botzi. These two are the main options for a more polished atmosphere.

items.name: Doloma
items.description: More alternative music and atmosphere. Located higher up in the alley.

items.name: Mantalou
items.description: Together with Doloma, the go-to spots for a more alternative crowd in the upper part of the alley.

items.name: Drakakis
items.description: A mezedopoleio (small plates bar) on the same street. A bit pricey but a great spot — and you can't get more central than this.

items.name: GRADO
items.description: The place for late-night dancing. Normally runs two floors: upstairs Greek music, downstairs international.
items.note: Ask if a reservation is needed.

areas.intro: The most beautiful village to wander through — and its scene has grown a lot in recent years.

items.name: Mosaiko
items.description: A must in Artemonas. A great mezedopoleio with a lovely atmosphere.

items.name: Diachroniko
items.description: A casual bar on the way to Mosaiko. Might catch your eye — worth a quick stop.

food.label: Food
food.intro: Sifnos is the birthplace of Nikolaos Tselementes — the father of Greek cuisine. The island has a strong culinary identity you shouldn't miss.

items.name: To Kelari
items.description: One of the best places to try authentic Sifnian cooking.

items.name: Tsikali
items.description: A taverna right on Vathi beach. Perfect for a long lunch after swimming.

items.name: Chrysopigi
items.description: A taverna right on Chrysopigi beach. Great sea views and the iconic church as backdrop.

localFood.label: Traditional Foods & Flavours
localFood.intro: The must-try foods and products of Sifnos:

items.name: Mastelo
items.description: Baby goat slow-cooked in red wine and dill inside a lidded clay pot of the same name (shaped like a casserole dish). The ultimate Sifnian recipe.

items.name: Revythada
items.description: Chickpeas soaked in rainwater and slow-cooked for many hours with onion until they turn creamy and silky. Served with a squeeze of lemon and crusty bread — pure bliss.

items.name: Revythokeftedes
items.description: Chickpea fritters — falafel before it was cool.

items.name: Kaparosalata
items.description: The island is covered in wild caper bushes hanging off stone walls. The caper salad is made with plenty of onion and some say it tastes a bit like stifado because of it.

items.name: (Xino)myzithra
items.description: A soft white cheese that is incredible and pairs perfectly with a Greek salad. Ask for it instead of feta — it'll likely be the local version.

items.name: Manoura
items.description: A strong aged cheese ripened in red wine, with a dark crust of wine sediment on the outside. It looks like mud on the rind — but that's where all the flavour is. Do not skip this.

items.name: Veniou Bakery
items.description: Handmade bougatsa and cheese pies in Kamares. The perfect stop right off the ferry.

items.name: Grigoris
items.description: The best traditional sweets on the island: amygdalota (almond macaroons), oven biscuits, aniseed rings and wine biscuits.

activities.label: Activities
activities.intro: From island cruises to hiking through ancient mines — what to do on Sifnos beyond the beach.

items.name: Boat Tour around Sifnos
items.description: Full-day cruise around the island — secluded coves, swim stops, lunch on the boat. Usually departs from Kamares or Platy Gialos. The best way to see Sifnos from a different angle.

items.name: Horse riding
items.description: Guided rides from a dedicated riding centre. Great for those who want to see Sifnos from a different trail.

items.name: Farm visit
items.description: Experience at a local farm — cheeses, dairy products, and a taste of the island's agricultural tradition.

subsections.label: Sunset
subsections.intro: Two very different experiences — one easy by car, one that requires a hike.

items.name: Agios Symeon
items.description: Drive up to Agios Symeon — just 10 minutes from Kamares. Incredible views with no effort; the road goes all the way up. Popular spot — go early.

items.name: Profitis Ilias o Apsilos
items.description: The highest point on the island. ~1-hour hike from the village. Bring water and proper shoes — the reward is a panoramic 360° view.

subsections.label: Hiking
subsections.intro: Sifnos has an excellent network of waymarked trails (Sifnos Trails) — from easy strolls to full-day routes. Bring water and good shoes.

items.name: Agios Silivestros & the Mines
items.description: Hike in the north of the island, up to the chapel of Agios Silivestros and the old mines. Historic landscape — this is where the ancient Sifnians extracted gold and silver, which paid for the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi.

items.name: Profitis Ilias o Apsilos
items.description: Uphill hike to the highest point on the island. Best done early morning or towards sunset.

items.name: Kamares → Kastro
items.description: Traditional crossing from the port to the medieval Kastro, through the mountain villages. Stop whenever you like — it passes through all the central villages.

history.label: History
history.intro: A short look at Sifnos's past — from the ancient mines to the modern era.

chapters.title: Antiquity — Gold and Silver
chapters.body: In antiquity Sifnos was one of the wealthiest Cycladic islands, thanks to its gold and silver mines in the north. With this wealth the Sifnians built the famous Siphnian Treasury at Delphi (~525 BC) — one of the most striking dedications in the sanctuary. According to myth, when the Sifnians stopped dedicating gold to Apollo, the god flooded their mines with the sea.

chapters.title: Byzantine & Venetian Period
chapters.body: From 1207 Sifnos passed into the hands of the Venetian Da Corogna family, who built the Kastro — the medieval fortified settlement that still stands today. The Kastro served for centuries as a defence against pirate raids.

chapters.title: Piracy
chapters.body: From the 13th to the 18th century, the Aegean islands were exposed to pirate raids. On Sifnos, the villages were built in the interior, away from the beaches, precisely for this reason. The narrow alleys, dead-end lanes, and tight-knit village layout are all defensive features.

chapters.title: Ottoman Period
chapters.body: From 1617 to 1821 Sifnos was under Ottoman rule but enjoyed relative autonomy due to its distance from the main administrative centres. During this period the island developed important traditions in seafaring and pottery.

chapters.title: Modern Era
chapters.body: In the 19th and 20th centuries the economy was based primarily on pottery (Sifnian Tsoukalades travelled across Greece selling clay vessels) and shipping. Today tourism dominates, but Sifnos still holds tightly to its traditions — gastronomy, panigyria, ceramics, and a strong local community.

practical.label: Practical
practical.intro: Everything practical you need for your visit to Sifnos.

items.title: Ferry
items.description: Sifnos is connected to Piraeus via daily routes (conventional ferries ~5 hours, high-speed ~2.5–3 hours). It also connects to Milos, Serifos, Kimolos, Folegandros and Santorini. Book tickets in advance for August.

items.title: Buses (KTEL)
items.description: KTEL Sifnou serves all main villages (Kamares, Apollonia, Artemonas, Kastro, Platy Gialos, Faros, Cherronisos, Vathy). Frequency is good in summer. All routes pass through Apollonia.

items.title: Parking
items.description: In the medieval villages (Apollonia, Artemonas, Kastro) car access is restricted. Park outside and walk in. In summer parking is tight — go early or use the bus.

items.title: Water
items.description: Tap water is NOT potable on Sifnos. Buy bottled water or ask for drinking-water fountains in the villages. Many restaurants serve filtered water.

items.title: Supermarkets
items.description: The largest supermarkets are in Apollonia and Kamares. Smaller grocers exist in almost every village. Generally open daily in summer.

items.title: Weather & Wind
items.description: When the north wind (meltemi) blows hard, move to Faros, Vathi or Platy Gialos. These beaches face South-East or South-West and stay much calmer. Always ask a local for the forecast too.

items.title: Ask the Locals
items.description: Always ask locals for tips, weather updates and any festivals or village celebrations happening during your stay. If you find a panigiri (religious feast), go — it's an experience.

culture.label: Culture
culture.intro: From summer panigyria (saint festivals) to museums and ceramic workshops — Sifnos has a living culture worth exploring.

subsections.label: Panigyria
subsections.intro: Food, wine, and dancing till dawn. The traditional saint festivals of Sifnos are some of the best in the Cyclades. Always ask locals for current times and locations — some dates shift year to year.

items.name: Panagia Chrysopigi
items.description: The most important festival on the island. Procession of the icon followed by an open-air celebration in the churchyard.

items.name: Prophet Elias
items.description: Festival at the highest point of Sifnos. Uphill trail, but the view and atmosphere are well worth the climb.

items.name: Panagia of Poulati
items.description: Festival at the church above Poulati. The busiest panigyri of August.

items.name: Agios Symeon
items.description: Festival at the small chapel of Agios Symeon with a magnificent view down to Kamares. Quieter than the August festivals.

items.name: Stavros
items.description: Local festivals at chapels dedicated to the Holy Cross. The slow closing of the Sifnos summer.

subsections.label: Events
subsections.intro: From food festivals to street parties — cultural events organised by local associations and friends of the island.

items.name: Nikolaos Tselementes Cycladic Gastronomy Festival
items.description: Gastronomy festival honouring Nikolaos Tselementes, the Sifnian chef who wrote the first modern Greek cookbook. Workshops, seminars, and dinners by top chefs.

items.name: Radioactive Street Party
items.description: Annual street party by local radio station Radioactive. Music, drinks, and half the island out in the street.

items.name: Mousifando
items.description: Music festival organised by the Sifnos Cultural Association, featuring local and visiting artists.

subsections.label: Pottery
subsections.intro: Sifnians have long been known as 'Tsoukalades' — master potters and exporters of clay cookware. The tradition lives on in working workshops across the island. The most authentic souvenir is a clay cooking vessel (tsoukali or gastra).

items.name: Keramika 'I Dyskoli'
items.description: One of the most traditional workshops on the island, in one of its most picturesque settings — right by the sea in Cherronisos. Authentic Sifnian pottery on the wheel.

subsections.label: Museums & Sites
subsections.intro: Few but excellent — Sifnos had an important role in antiquity, with silver mines and a treasury at Delphi.

items.name: Agios Andreas Archaeological Site
items.description: Ancient acropolis from the Geometric period with sweeping views over the whole island. Important finds and a small archaeological museum on site. One of the most beautiful archaeological sites in the Cyclades.

items.name: Sifnos Folklore Museum
items.description: Collection of traditional Sifnian clothing, tools, and everyday objects. On the main square of Apollonia.
